inputs.need:
I am a critical care physiotherapist and research lead in a 28-bed mixed medical and surgical intensive care unit. Eighteen months ago we introduced an early mobilisation bundle: daily screening for readiness, mobilisation to sitting or standing within 72 hours when safe, and recording the ICU Mobility Scale every day. Adherence is patchy: when we checked last spring, only 46 percent of eligible patient-days had mobilisation documented. At the same time we measure muscle strength with the MRC sum score at ICU discharge for every patient ventilated for more than 48 hours, and about a quarter leave the unit with ICU-acquired weakness, a score below 48.

We plan a case-control study nested in our ICU clinical information system: cases would be patients discharged with ICU-acquired weakness since the bundle started, controls patients without it, and the exposure would be the number of days in the first five eligible days on which mobilisation was missed. The ICU director also wants to know two other things: whether the ICU Mobility Scale on day 3 could flag patients at risk early, and how many extra ICU days weakness adds.

I need help defining cases and controls, matching or adjusting for illness severity, sedation and length of ventilation, handling the fact that sicker patients are both less mobilised and weaker, the number of cases we need, and how to stop the director's extra questions from taking over the study. We have a research nurse two days a week and no external funding.
inputs.constraints: No external funding. Research nurse 2 days per week until August 2027. Data only from the ICU clinical information system and hospital discharge summaries; no new measurements on patients.
localFacts: The mobilisation bundle started in March 2025; daily mobilisation status and the ICU Mobility Scale are recorded in the ICU clinical information system.
The MRC sum score is recorded at ICU discharge for every patient ventilated for more than 48 hours; about 25 percent score below 48.
A check in spring 2026 found mobilisation documented on 46 percent of eligible patient-days.
The research ethics board approved a waiver of consent for this chart-based study on 2026-09-16 (approval REB-2026-0931).
The ICU director approved release of the clinical information system extract on 2026-09-18 (approval ICU-DIR-2026-12).

response.title: Missed early mobilisation and ICU-acquired weakness in a mixed intensive care unit: a nested case-control study
response.subtitle: Bundle adherence as exposure; ICU-acquired weakness as case status
response.statement: Eighteen months after an early mobilisation bundle began in a 28-bed mixed intensive care unit, mobilisation is documented on 46 percent of eligible patient-days and about a quarter of patients ventilated for more than 48 hours leave with ICU-acquired weakness. The unit wants to know whether missed mobilisation in the first five eligible days is associated with weakness at ICU discharge, using cases and controls from its clinical information system, while two secondary questions from the director (early identification on day 3 and extra ICU days) must not distort the main study.
response.whoAffected: Adults ventilated for more than 48 hours in the unit, their families, bedside nurses, physiotherapists and intensivists.
response.whatHurts: ICU-acquired weakness delays recovery and independence for months; missed mobilisation may contribute, but sicker patients are both less mobilised and weaker, which makes the association hard to read.
response.currentPractice: A bundle with daily readiness screening and mobilisation within 72 hours when safe; documentation spread across several places.
response.whyNow: Eighteen months of bundle data exist, adherence is poor, and the director wants evidence before investing in more physiotherapy staffing.
response.constraints: No external funding. Research nurse 2 days per week until August 2027. Data only from the ICU clinical information system and hospital discharge summaries; no new measurements on patients.
response.patientCenteredGoal: Patients leave intensive care strong enough to recover function, and mobilisation is offered whenever it is safe.
response.summary: Problem framed as a nested case-control study with two contained secondary questions.

records.title: Early mobilisation in mechanically ventilated adults and ICU-acquired weakness: a randomised trial
records.authors: Brennan-Adeyemi C, Solberg-Mwangi T, Iqbal-Fontaine R
records.abstract: We randomly allocated 200 adults expected to be ventilated for more than 48 hours to early mobilisation led by physiotherapists from the first day of stability, or to usual care with mobilisation when clinicians judged it appropriate. ICU-acquired weakness at ICU discharge, defined as an MRC sum score below 48, occurred in 27 percent with early mobilisation and 41 percent with usual care. Functional independence at hospital discharge was 52 percent and 38 percent. Adverse events during mobilisation occurred in 1 percent of sessions, none serious. The trial was at two centres with experienced physiotherapy teams.

records.title: Early mobilisation in critically ill adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis of muscle strength and function
records.authors: Takahashi-Oyelaran M, Delgado-Hurst P, Nkemelu-Strand A
records.abstract: We included 16 randomised trials of early mobilisation in critically ill adults. Early mobilisation reduced ICU-acquired weakness (risk ratio 0.70, 95 percent CI 0.55 to 0.89) and improved function at discharge, with no difference in mortality. Trials varied widely in the timing and dose of mobilisation, and most compared an enhanced programme with little mobilisation rather than with partial adherence to a protocol. Adverse events were rare and none was fatal. Certainty was moderate for weakness and low for function, and no trial reported outcomes beyond hospital discharge.

records.title: Barriers to mobilisation in intensive care: a multicentre point-prevalence study
records.abstract: On two survey days, 38 intensive care units recorded whether each patient was mobilised and the main reason if not. Patients were mobilised on 36 percent of patient-days. Sedation was the most common barrier, recorded on 42 percent of days without mobilisation, followed by haemodynamic instability and staff availability. Units with a dedicated physiotherapist and a daily sedation interruption protocol mobilised more patients. Barrier recording depended on staff judgement and may have been inconsistent between units, and weekend days were not sampled.

records.title: Illness severity and the association between immobility and ICU-acquired weakness: a cohort analysis
records.authors: Haddad-Kowalski S, Ferreira-Nnamdi O, Lund-Achebe K
records.abstract: In 640 ventilated adults, we examined the association between days without mobilisation in the first week and ICU-acquired weakness at discharge. The crude odds ratio was 3.1 per three days without mobilisation, which fell to 1.4 (95 percent CI 0.9 to 2.2) after adjustment for illness severity score, days of deep sedation, sepsis and corticosteroid use. Sicker patients were both less often mobilised and more often weak. The authors conclude that observational estimates are strongly confounded by severity and recommend restriction to patients eligible for mobilisation on each day.

records.title: The ICU Mobility Scale on day 3 as a marker of later ICU-acquired weakness: a diagnostic accuracy study
records.abstract: We assessed whether the ICU Mobility Scale on day 3 identified 312 ventilated adults who would have ICU-acquired weakness at discharge. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.71. At a threshold below 3, sensitivity was 68 percent and specificity 64 percent. Patients who were sedated on day 3 could not be scored and were excluded, which may have inflated accuracy. The authors suggest the scale is too inaccurate on its own to target interventions but may add to a risk score.

records.title: Length of stay attributable to ICU-acquired weakness: a matched analysis
records.abstract: We matched 220 patients with ICU-acquired weakness to 220 without it on age, admission diagnosis, illness severity and days of ventilation. Weakness was associated with 4.2 additional ICU days and 9 additional hospital days. Costs were not reported directly, but the authors note that ICU days are the most expensive part of an admission. Matching could not remove differences in sedation practice, and patients who died in the ICU were excluded, so the attributable stay may be overestimated. The analysis did not examine mobilisation.

records.title: Nurses' and physiotherapists' views of early mobilisation in intensive care: a focus group study
records.abstract: We held focus groups with 26 nurses and physiotherapists in three intensive care units. Staff supported early mobilisation but feared dislodging lines and tubes, particularly at night and at weekends when fewer physiotherapists were present. Responsibility for deciding that a patient was ready to mobilise was often unclear. Staff described documentation of mobilisation as incomplete because it was recorded in several places. Participants suggested a single daily readiness decision recorded by the bedside nurse, with the physiotherapist confirming the plan at the morning round.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Randomised trials show that early mobilisation reduces ICU-acquired weakness, but they compare mobilising with not mobilising, not partial adherence to a bundle. An observational cohort shows the crude association between immobility and weakness is largely explained by illness severity and sedation, which is the central threat for a case-control design; counting only days when a patient was eligible helps. The day-3 mobility scale is a modest marker, and weakness is associated with about four more ICU days. Barriers and staff views point to sedation and unclear responsibility.
response.gradeRationale: Moderate certainty that mobilisation prevents weakness from randomised evidence; low certainty for the observational associations that the local study will extend.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; four claims; certainty moderate for the effect of mobilisation.

steps.note: Appraisal of seven retrieved records (S13); certainty 'moderate' over inspected records (G1). The diagnostic accuracy record ingested as kind 'grey' (its provider label maps to no safe kind) is annotated as observational.

response.designSummary: Nested case-control study with two controls per case matched on ventilation duration band and admission quarter; conditional logistic regression.
response.sampleSize: About 25 percent of about 300 eligible patients a year have weakness, so about 150 cases are expected from March 2025 to June 2027. With two controls per case and 40 percent of controls missing at least two eligible days, about 100 cases give 80 percent power at two-sided alpha 0.05 to detect an odds ratio of 2.0, and about 140 cases an odds ratio of 1.8, before allowing for adjustment. The study is therefore sized for moderate associations only, and a null result will be reported with its interval.

response.secondaryAnalysis: Difference in ICU days between cases and matched controls, described with a bootstrap interval and valued at the ICU day rate; area under the curve for the day-3 scale among patients who could be scored; missed days by day of week.
response.missingData: Days without documentation are analysed as a separate category and in a sensitivity analysis as missed; no imputation of case status.
response.multiplicity: One primary association; secondary analyses descriptive.
response.software: R (survival package for conditional logistic regression).
